story: On October 20, 2003, astrophysicists J. Richard Gott III and Mario Jurić of Princeton University announced a discovery that shattered previous cosmic records: the Sloan Great Wall. Uncovered through the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's three-dimensional redshift measurements, this vast structure lies about one billion light-years from Earth. Spanning a breathtaking 1.37 billion light-years across space, it eclipsed the previously known CfA Great Wall by roughly 80 percent. Rather than a solid physical barrier, the Sloan Great Wall is a colossal thread of the cosmic web, linking thousands of galaxies, clusters, and massive superclusters like SCl 126 and SCl 111 along unseen scaffolding of dark matter. Its sheer scale offered astronomers an unprecedented cosmic laboratory, testing theoretical boundaries of how matter clustered after the Big Bang.
angle: A cosmic thread of galaxies spanning 1.37 billion light-years—so colossal that light traveling at 186,000 miles per second takes over a billion years just to cross it.
disputed: Constellation location: S1 states the wall lies within Corvus, Hydra, and Centaurus, while S5 claims it is located toward Corona Borealis. Scripts should omit the constellation reference or state celestial coordinates.

Physical unity: S1 notes that a 2011 study suggested the wall may be a chance alignment of three separate structures rather than a single continuous physical object. Scripts should attribute this: 'according to later analysis, it may be a chance alignment of three distinct structures'.

Absolute size ranking: S7 claimed it was the largest observed structure in 2003, whereas S1 lists it as the sixth largest known today, and S5 contradicts itself regarding whether it is larger or smaller than the Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall. Scripts should describe it as 'one of the largest known galaxy structures'.
